description: We enjoy building practical solutions that combine engineering, technology and healthcare, and we are especially interested in challenges involving human health, space applications, sensing, data analysis and intelligent systems.
summary:
Apogee is a proposed astronaut health-monitoring system designed to address Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS), a condition associated with long-duration spaceflight that can affect astronauts' vision and potentially compromise mission safety.

Our solution combines a non-invasive, earbud-shaped acoustic sensor concept with an intelligent monitoring platform. By studying acoustic responses and subtle physiological changes within the ear canal, Apogee aims to explore potential indicators of health changes associated with SANS.

The software visualizes astronaut health data, identifies changes that require attention, and communicates alerts to both the astronaut and Mission Control.

Beyond monitoring, Apogee proposes an adaptive task-management system that recommends adjustments to daily activities based on the astronaut's condition. For example, visually demanding maintenance could be replaced with a less demanding inventory task following Mission Control review.

Our goal is to support earlier awareness of potential health risks, improve astronaut safety, and enable more informed decision-making during long-duration space missions.
details:
Apogee — Project Details

The Problem

Long-duration spaceflight exposes astronauts to physiological changes caused by altered gravity, including Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS). This condition can involve optic disc swelling, flattening of the eyeball, and changes in visual performance. Approximately 70% of astronauts aboard the International Space Station experience some degree of swelling at the back of their eyes.

Visual impairment can compromise tasks requiring precision, such as equipment maintenance, scientific experiments, and spacecraft operations. Understanding these changes and their relationship with intracranial fluid dynamics remains an important NASA research priority.

Our Solution

Apogee proposes an integrated astronaut health-monitoring system combining a non-invasive in-ear sensing device with a mission management software platform.

The proposed wearable incorporates a miniature acoustic speaker and microphone to investigate changes in ear-canal acoustic reflectance. A controlled sound stimulus is emitted and its reflected response is recorded. By comparing the acoustic response against each astronaut's individual baseline, the system aims to explore physiological changes potentially associated with fluid redistribution during spaceflight.

The hardware concept also considers acoustic calibration, ear-seal verification, pressure sensing, onboard signal processing, and wireless communication.

Software and Mission Integration

Apogee translates monitoring information into an intuitive interface designed for both astronauts and Mission Control.

The platform is designed to:

  • Display individual astronaut health profiles and monitoring indicators.
  • Visualize historical measurements and physiological trends.
  • Highlight changes that may require further medical evaluation.
  • Relate monitoring trends to previously performed mission activities.
  • Suggest adjustments to task assignments based on the astronaut's condition.
  • Communicate task recommendations and schedule updates to the astronaut.

For example, when a concerning change is identified, the system may recommend postponing a visually demanding precision-maintenance task and assigning a lower-demand activity, such as inventory management, following review by Mission Control.

Innovation and Impact

Apogee combines an exploratory ear-based sensing approach with personalized longitudinal monitoring and operational task adaptation.

Rather than merely displaying physiological measurements, the project explores how health information could support safer mission planning and more informed decisions during long-duration spaceflight.

Its intended benefits include increased awareness of physiological changes, reduced monitoring burden, improved communication between astronauts and Mission Control, and greater flexibility in daily mission operations.

Scientific Basis and Limitations

The concept draws on NASA Human Research Program resources and published studies on SANS, microgravity-related fluid shifts, tympanic membrane displacement, and ear-canal acoustic measurements.

The project currently represents a proposed sensing architecture and software demonstration. Acoustic measurements have not been clinically validated by our team as a method for diagnosing SANS or directly measuring intracranial pressure. Any illustrative measurements or alerts in the demonstration must be distinguished from real astronaut medical data.

Future development would require physical sensor prototyping, acoustic calibration, controlled physiological studies, and comparison with established clinical assessment methods.
